result:
**Verdict.** The zero-joint export is not a partly articulated model waiting to be completed. The exporter found no joint mates it recognized, so it fused every occurrence into one link. That is an assembly-structure or mate-naming problem in Onshape, and it should be fixed there. The ZIP is a valid, pinned source for geometry, per-part mass and inertia, and nothing more. Any articulation inferred from it is a fit with residual error and ownership risk, never a CAD assertion. Treat the reconstruction below as a fallback and an independent audit, not the primary path.

## Articulation

**Primary path: re-export with mates exposed.** Onshape-to-robot emits a joint only for a mate it recognizes by the configured joint prefix at the assembly level it walks. One link named `body_subassy` with zero joints means the exported document either is that sub-assembly or wraps the whole robot in one rigid sub-assembly, and no joint mate was visible under a recognized name. Ask the CAD owner to do four things at the level being exported. Name the 18 motor mates and the 12 tree-side passive pivots with the joint prefix. Name the six rod-to-tibia closures with the exporter's closing-mate convention so the loop is explicit rather than inferred. Add frame mates for the six foot contact points and the IMU. Re-export at a pinned version and record document, version and microversion IDs. The capture pose can stay arbitrary. This is the strongest path because the mate connector carries the bearing axis and origin exactly as designed, and it is likely under an hour of CAD work.

**Fallback: reconstruction from robot.pkl.** Use it if the re-export is delayed, and run it anyway so the re-export has something independent to agree with.

- **Check for occurrence paths before inferring anything.** If robot.pkl or the .part JSON carries the assembly occurrence path per instance, sub-assembly boundaries give rigid groups directly and ownership needs no geometry. This one check removes most of the risk.
- **Take axes from instanced feature meshes, not from the fused body.** Among the 59 unique meshes, identify bearings, pins, motor housings and output flanges. Compute each mesh's symmetry axis once in its own frame from the principal directions of its geometry. Every instance transform then yields a world axis line. Eighteen motor instances give the actuated axes. Bearing and pin instances give the passive pivots. Cylinder fits on the merged geometry are strictly worse. If the femur and pushlever motor axes are parallel and close, the lines alone cannot tell the two joints apart. Ownership from the next step does.
- **Use the arbitrary pose as evidence.** Six legs are six copies at different configurations. For two part types that occur once per leg, compute the relative transform between them in every leg. Constant across legs means the same rigid body. Varying by a rotation about one line means exactly one joint between them, and that line is the axis, recovered without touching the bearing mesh. Part IDs from the .part JSON establish which instances are the same design across legs. Left and right legs may be mirror families. A mirrored instance carries a reflection in its transform, so test the determinant and treat each family separately.
- **Decide pushlever motor ownership by that test, not by keyword.** Its housing is constant relative to the coxa across legs if coxa-mounted, and constant relative to the femur if femur-mounted. The answer moves a 191 g mass between links that themselves weigh around a hundred grams, so it dominates femur inertia and the third motor's load. The historical default-to-chassis rule must not run on this part or on any part with once-per-leg multiplicity.
- **Split each motor by function.** Housing mass goes to the parent link. Rotor inertia goes into the actuator armature, not into the child link. An output flange goes to the child only if it is a separate mesh.
- **Verify the loop before claiming a mimic.** Extract the four pivot centres per leg and compute the four link lengths. Only a true parallelogram makes the knee and rod angles linear in the pushlever angle, and linear is all a native mimic constraint represents. The export changed lengths, so the historical parallelogram assumption is void until re-measured. Two passive coordinates need two constraints. A mimic on the knee alone leaves the rod free and the closure open. Measure the rod-end gap in simulation across the full range and record it as the closure evidence.
- **Never take joint zero or the base frame from the capture pose.** Define a geometric zero per joint from features, such as the femur axis parallel to the coxa mounting plane, and compute each leg's capture angle relative to it. Store those only as capture angles. Place the base frame by a documented chassis feature, not the CAD origin. The URDF axis sign is a recorded convention. Encoder zero, motor sign and reset pose are separate records, and the first two stay blank until hardware calibration.
- **Prove it by round trip.** Assemble the tree, set the extracted capture angles, and reproduce all 1753 instance transforms from the export. Residual means wrong ownership or wrong axis. Nothing about the articulation is admitted without this test passing.

## Fail-closed criteria and audits

These are new admission thresholds for a new lineage, not edits to any existing gate. Fix them in the admission report before anyone measures against them.

| Check | Fail if |
|---|---|
| Round-trip residual | any instance off by more than 0.5 mm or 0.1 degrees |
| Axis agreement across leg pairs | direction spread above 0.2 degrees or line offset above 0.2 mm |
| Ownership provenance | any part assigned by keyword or by default to chassis |
| Multiplicity | any part occurring six or more times left unassigned to legs |
| Joint evidence | a joint inferred with no motor, bearing or pin instance on that interface |
| Parallelogram | opposite link lengths differ by more than 0.5 mm |
| Mass closure | body masses do not sum to the fused 5.1476 kg before overrides |
| Inertia validity | tensor not symmetric positive definite, or principal moments violate the triangle inequality |
| Inertia frame | uniform-density recomputation from the STL disagrees with pkl principal directions, for parts with distinct moments |
| Repair magnitude | any principal moment changed more than 5% without a named cause |
| Instance transform | determinant not plus one, or orthonormality error above 1e-6 |
| Mesh integrity | non-manifold, negative signed volume, or a body span outside plausible metres |
| Capture-pose penetration | distinct bodies overlap beyond bearing clearance |
| Collider set | fasteners kept as colliders, or adjacent-link filtering unspecified |

**Tensor audit.** Compose each body from its parts with the parallel-axis theorem in the body frame. First establish the pkl convention. Recompute each unique part's inertia from its STL at uniform density and compare principal directions. Agreement only after a frame change tells you the convention, and this catches the most common silent inertia error. Solid parts should match closely. Shells such as the motor housings will not, and that mismatch is the signature of mass needing an override. Write the full symmetric tensor at the centre of mass into URDF with zero rotation. Log every repair with before, after and cause.

**Mesh audit.** For the 59 unique meshes record volume, surface area, manifoldness, signed-volume sign and a per-file hash. For the 1753 instances validate the transform and treat any reflection as a mirrored occurrence. URDF cannot express a reflection in an origin, so bake it into a new mesh file with corrected normals. Record the CP437 to UTF-8 filename decoding map in the manifest so the ZIP resolves reproducibly.

**Collider audit.** A single link with 1753 collision elements is not usable. Per rigid body use one convex hull of the structural parts, or a small convex decomposition where concavity matters, and drop fasteners from collision entirely. The foot shape changed, so the foot collider is rebuilt from the new geometry with its fit error recorded. Filter self-collision among rod, femur and tibia, otherwise contacts fight the closure. Visuals keep the full meshes.

## Bounds, materials, lineage and claims

**Provisional bounds.** Rank four sources per joint and publish which one governs. First, a CAD interference sweep on the reconstructed model with neighbours at rest. Second, the four-bar toggle limit where crank and rod align and mechanical advantage vanishes, with a margin kept well inside it. Third, the motor range from the datasheet, which for a multi-turn actuator is not a limit. Fourth, any explicit hard-stop part visible in CAD, recorded as a CAD assertion. Each joint gets the raw angle, the margin, the provisional limit and the line "physical stop: not asserted". Cables and harness are absent from CAD and can only tighten these. Only measured stops promote a bound.

**What URDF can hold.** Link mass, centre of mass and the full inertia tensor. Joint axis, limits, and scalar damping and friction. Visual colour. Nothing else. No density, no contact friction, no compliance. So the material breakdown feeds three destinations. Link inertials go into URDF. Foot friction and restitution go into a physics material on the foot colliders, as a range for randomization rather than a point, and that range is a documented assumption until measured. Torque-speed, overload, gear ratio and reflected rotor inertia belong to the actuator model in the adapter. Compliance of long printed links is not representable and is recorded as a sim-to-real risk.

**Material breakdown without material names.** Compute density as pkl mass over STL volume for each unique part and bin it. Aluminium sits near 2.70, steel near 7.85, printed plastics between 1.04 and 1.27, nylon near 1.15, with PCB and cells in their own bands. Report mass, volume, density, inferred class, confidence and instance count per unique part. Zero or default densities mean an unassigned material and must be listed. Before declaring names absent, have a worker check the Onshape part metadata endpoint, since the exporter may simply not have requested them.

**Mass ledger.** Three columns per body and per category: CAD nominal, corrected with sourced overrides, and measured, left blank until the robot is weighed.

| Item | kg |
|---|---|
| Fused export | 5.148 |
| Motor override, 18 units from about 0.062 to 0.191 | +2.32 |
| Corrected estimate | about 7.47 |
| Historical full assembly | 8.261 |
| Unexplained gap | about 0.79 |

Attribute the gap by category before anyone reasons about torque margin or payload. Missing battery, electronics or cabling, and shortened links are the candidates, and the export cannot tell you which.

**Claim hygiene.** Everything in the ZIP is a CAD assertion at assumed densities in an arbitrary pose. The 191 g motor figure is external and must cite its source. Hardware evidence that does not yet exist: weighed mass, encoder zeros, motor signs, measured stops, foot friction, and any admission pass. The physical candidate's torque-speed and overload dynamics remain provisional. The admission report keeps the two classes in separate sections.

**Lineage and packaging.** The manifest pins the ZIP hash, exporter version, Onshape document, version and microversion IDs, the filename decoding map and per-mesh hashes, and labels the asset as mesh-only, unarticulated and not Isaac-ready. A reconstructed asset is a new lineage with a new task ID. The C-study geometry, the serial-v2 characterization and the archived mock contracts stay untouched. Each step carries its update record under the project site contract, and root alone integrates.

**Recommended order.** Request the mate-exposed re-export today. In parallel, run the fallback reconstruction on the current ZIP as the independent audit the re-export must agree with. Finish the tensor, mesh and material audits on the current ZIP now, since they do not depend on articulation. Admit no articulated asset until the round-trip test, the axis agreement and the parallelogram check all pass, and keep the mesh-only import labelled as a geometry and mass source, not Isaac-ready.
